Red wine grapes.Merlot: Soft, plummy grape of Bordeaux's right bank. The name probably comes from merle, French for blackbird, the bird that loved to eat the grapes.
Red wine grapes.Cabernet Sauvignon: A cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, found by chance in 17th-century France. Thick skins make bold wines and it is the backbone of Bordeaux's left bank.
Red wine grapes.Pinot Noir: A fussy, thin-skinned grape that thrives in Burgundy's cool climate. It is among the hardest to grow, and it is the star of the film Sideways.
Red wine grapes.Syrah: Known as Shiraz in Australia, it is the same grape. Genetic tests showed it descends from two obscure French varieties.
Red wine grapes.Malbec: Once a minor Bordeaux blending grape, now Argentina's signature wine; dark purple wines come mostly from Mendoza's high-altitude vineyards.
Red wine grapes.Zinfandel: California's heritage grape, DNA-matched to Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski and Italy's Primitivo. Not to be confused with sweet pink 'white zinfandel'.
Red wine grapes.Tempranillo: Spain's noble grape, whose name comes from temprano, 'early', because it ripens early. It is the backbone of Rioja.
Red wine grapes.Sangiovese: Italy's most planted red grape; its name is thought to come from Latin for 'blood of Jupiter'. It is the grape of Chianti.
Red wine grapes.Grenache: A heat-loving grape from Spain, called Garnacha there. It is a key part of Châteauneuf-du-Pape and makes excellent rosé too.
Red wine grapes.Nebbiolo: Piedmont's late-ripening grape behind Barolo and Barbaresco. Its name is thought to come from nebbia, Italian for fog, which blankets the harvest.
Red wine grapes.Gamay: The grape of Beaujolais; in 1395 a duke of Burgundy banned it as 'very bad and disloyal', and it still thrives just south of his region.
Red wine grapes.Carménère: Once thought lost after Europe's phylloxera, it was mistaken for Merlot in Chile until DNA tests in 1994. Chile is now its home, with a spicy character.
Red wine grapes.Barbera: Piedmont's everyday red, with bright acidity and cherry notes. It is so versatile that locals drink it daily with pasta.
Red wine grapes.Chardonnay: A trap: Chardonnay is green-skinned and white. It makes Chablis, white Burgundy, and is a main grape in Champagne.
Red wine grapes.Sauvignon Blanc: A zippy white grape from Bordeaux and the Loire. It is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, and its name means 'wild white'.
Red wine grapes.Riesling: Germany's great white grape, from the Rhine. Its wines range from bone-dry to very sweet, and they can age for decades.
Red wine grapes.Pinot Grigio: The same grape as Pinot Gris, making a white. Its skin is grayish-pink, but the juice is clear, so the wine is pale.
Red wine grapes.Viognier: A white grape from the Rhône, which nearly vanished in the 1960s, with only a few acres left. Now popular worldwide.
Red wine grapes.Chenin Blanc: A white grape from the Loire, with high acidity, making everything from dry to sweet to sparkling wines. Called Steen in South Africa.
Red wine grapes.Gewürztraminer: A pink-skinned grape that makes white wine, with lychee and rose aromas. Its name means spicy Traminer, after Tramin in northern Italy.
Red wine grapes.Moscato: A white grape with a grapey, floral scent, and it tastes like the fruit. It is made into low-alcohol Asti and Moscato d'Asti fizz.
Red wine grapes.Albariño: Spain's Galician white grape, bright and salty, loved with seafood. It grows along the Rías Baixas coast in the north-west.
Red wine grapes.Sémillon: A white grape that makes Sauternes sweet wine when infected by noble rot. It also makes dry whites in Bordeaux and Australia.
Red wine grapes.Grüner Veltliner: Austria's signature white grape, with a peppery bite. Its name means 'green one of Veltlin', and it pairs with foods other wines struggle with.

National capitals in Asia.Beijing: The name means northern capital, and its Forbidden City palace complex has nearly 1,000 buildings.
National capitals in Asia.Seoul: The name literally means capital in Korean, and the city is home to about a fifth of South Koreans.

National capitals in Asia.Hanoi: Vietnam's capital has been a center of power since 1010, when the Ly dynasty founded Thang Long there.
National capitals in Asia.Manila: The Philippines' capital sits on a big bay, and Manila proper is far smaller than the sprawling metropolitan area around it.
National capitals in Asia.Jakarta: Indonesia is building a new capital, Nusantara, on Borneo, partly because Jakarta is sinking quickly.
National capitals in Asia.Kathmandu: Nepal's capital lies in a valley with seven UNESCO World Heritage sites.
National capitals in Asia.Dhaka: Bangladesh's capital is nicknamed the city of rickshaws and is one of the most densely populated cities on Earth.
National capitals in Asia.Kabul: Afghanistan's capital lies about 1,800 m up in the mountains, and has been a trade crossroads for millennia.
National capitals in Asia.Tehran: Iran's capital sits at the foot of the Alborz mountains and has been the capital since 1789.
National capitals in Asia.Ulaanbaatar: Mongolia's capital is the coldest national capital on Earth, and its name means Red Hero.
National capitals in Asia.Shanghai: A trap. It is China's largest city by population and a major port, but Beijing is the capital.
National capitals in Asia.Osaka: Japan's second-biggest metropolis is famous for its food, but Tokyo is the capital.
National capitals in Asia.Mumbai: India's financial capital and home of Bollywood is not the national capital, which is New Delhi.
National capitals in Asia.Karachi: It is Pakistan's biggest city and was its first capital, until Islamabad took over in the 1960s.
National capitals in Asia.Ho Chi Minh City: Formerly Saigon, it is Vietnam's biggest city, but Hanoi is the capital.
National capitals in Asia.Hong Kong: It is a special administrative region of China, not a national capital.
National capitals in Asia.Busan: South Korea's second-largest city and biggest port is not its capital, which is Seoul.
National capitals in Asia.Istanbul: Turkey's biggest city, once capital of the Ottoman Empire, is not the capital. Ankara has been since 1923.
National capitals in Asia.Dubai: The UAE's glitziest city is not the capital. That is Abu Dhabi, which holds most of its oil wealth.
National capitals in Asia.Almaty: It was Kazakhstan's capital until 1997, when the government moved north to Astana, but it is still the country's largest city.
National capitals in Asia.Yangon: Myanmar's biggest city was the capital until 2006, when the government moved to Naypyidaw.
National capitals in Asia.Kyoto: It was Japan's imperial capital for over a thousand years, until the emperor moved to Tokyo in 1868.

US states starting with a vowel.Alabama: Its name comes from the Alabama people, and Huntsville in the state helped build the rockets that sent Americans to the Moon.
US states starting with a vowel.Alaska: It is larger than Texas, California, and Montana combined, and its name comes from an Aleut word meaning mainland.
US states starting with a vowel.Arizona: It is the only state besides Hawaii to skip daylight saving time, and the Grand Canyon is its most famous sight.
US states starting with a vowel.Arkansas: Pronounced 'AR-kan-saw', it is home to the only active diamond mine in the US open to the public, Crater of Diamonds.
US states starting with a vowel.Idaho: The name was invented by a lobbyist who claimed it was a Shoshone word, and the fiction stuck.
US states starting with a vowel.Illinois: Its name comes from a French version of an Algonquian word for the people there, and Lincoln lived in its capital, Springfield.
US states starting with a vowel.Indiana: It means land of the Indians, and its biggest annual event is the Indianapolis 500 auto race.
US states starting with a vowel.Iowa: Its name is from the Ioway people, and the caucuses held here open the US presidential nomination process.
US states starting with a vowel.Ohio: It is the only state flag that isn't a rectangle, being a swallowtail pennant, and the state name comes from an Iroquois word for great river.
US states starting with a vowel.Oklahoma: It joined the Union in 1907, and the Land Run of 1889 saw thousands race to claim free land.
US states starting with a vowel.Oregon: The Oregon Trail ran about 2,000 miles to it, and Crater Lake here is the deepest lake in the country.
US states starting with a vowel.Utah: The Great Salt Lake lies here, and the state's name comes from the Ute people, with skiing renowned for its light powder.
US states starting with a vowel.Montana: Trap: it begins with a consonant, though its name comes from the Spanish word for mountain.
US states starting with a vowel.Texas: Trap: it begins with a T, and its name comes from a Caddo word, taysha, meaning friends.
US states starting with a vowel.Nevada: Trap: starts with N, and its name is Spanish for snow-covered, after the Sierra Nevada.
US states starting with a vowel.Georgia: Trap: begins with a G, and it was named for King George II of Great Britain.
US states starting with a vowel.Kansas: Trap: it begins with K, from the Kansa people, whose name is also the source of the Kansas River.
US states starting with a vowel.Maine: Trap: starts with M, and may be named after the French province of Maine or the term mainland.
US states starting with a vowel.Florida: Trap: it starts with an F, and Ponce de Leon named it La Florida, Spanish for flowery, after Easter in 1513.
US states starting with a vowel.Wyoming: Trap: it starts with W, and it was the first state to give women the vote, in 1869 as a territory.
US states starting with a vowel.Colorado: Trap: begins with a C, and it is Spanish for colored red, referring to the river's muddy water.
US states starting with a vowel.Vermont: Trap: it starts with a consonant, from the French vert mont, meaning green mountain.
US states starting with a vowel.Hawaii: Trap: begins with H, and it is the only state made entirely of islands, with a language that uses just 13 letters.
US states starting with a vowel.Kentucky: Trap: starts with K, and the Kentucky Derby has been run at Churchill Downs every year since 1875.

Places in South Korea.Seoul: The capital holds about a fifth of the country's people, and its Han River once powered an economic boom called the Miracle on the Han.
Places in South Korea.Busan: The country's second city and largest port, home to a huge film festival and colorful hillside villages.
Places in South Korea.Incheon: Its international airport is one of Asia's busiest, and General MacArthur's 1950 landing here turned the Korean War.
Places in South Korea.Jeju Island: A volcanic island known for haenyeo, female divers who free-dive for seafood into their 80s.
Places in South Korea.Daegu: A city famed for its apples and textile industry, and one of the hottest in the country.
Places in South Korea.Gyeongju: The ancient capital of the Silla kingdom, nicknamed a museum without walls for its royal tombs and temples.
Places in South Korea.Gangnam: This wealthy Seoul district was made globally famous in 2012 by Psy's song Gangnam Style.
Places in South Korea.Daejeon: A science and research hub where many Korean institutes and the Expo 93 were located.
Places in South Korea.Gwangju: The city of the 1980 democratic uprising, now known for its biennale of contemporary art.
Places in South Korea.Ulsan: A major industrial city and home of Hyundai's biggest car factory, the world's largest single car plant.
Places in South Korea.Pyeongchang: This mountain county hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics, and its Daegwallyeong plateau is famed for snow and sheep ranches.
Places in South Korea.Pyongyang: The capital of North Korea, not the south, with the Ryugyong Hotel pyramid.
Places in South Korea.Kaesong: A North Korean city just north of the DMZ, with a joint industrial zone once run with the South.
Places in South Korea.Osaka: A Japanese city known for street food, famed as the nation's kitchen.
Places in South Korea.Fukuoka: A Japanese city on Kyushu, near the Korean Peninsula but still in Japan.
Places in South Korea.Shenyang: A big northeastern Chinese city and capital of Liaoning province, once the Manchu capital, just across the border from North Korea.
Places in South Korea.Harbin: A Chinese city known for its giant ice and snow festival, with Russian-influenced architecture.
Places in South Korea.Vladivostok: The Russian Pacific port at the end of the Trans-Siberian Railway.
Places in South Korea.Kyoto: Japan's former capital for over a thousand years, with thousands of temples and shrines.
Places in South Korea.Okinawa: Japan's southernmost prefecture, an island chain with its own Ryukyu culture, not Korea.
Places in South Korea.Taipei: Taiwan's capital, once home to the world's tallest building, Taipei 101, completed in 2004.
Places in South Korea.Dalian: A Chinese port city on the Yellow Sea in Liaoning province, near the Korean Peninsula but not in South Korea.
Places in South Korea.Wonsan: A North Korean port on the east coast with a beach resort at Kalma, so it lies north of the border.
Places in South Korea.Nagasaki: A Japanese port city on Kyushu, the second to suffer an atomic bomb, in 1945.

Countries with just one land neighbour.Denmark: Only Germany borders it by land, on the Jutland peninsula, though it also has more than 400 islands.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Ireland: Only Northern Ireland, part of the UK, shares a land border with the Republic.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Canada: Its only land neighbour is the United States, and the border is the longest in the world between two countries.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Lesotho: A kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, one of only three countries fully enclaved by another.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Monaco: France is its only land neighbour, and it is a city-state on the Mediterranean.
Countries with just one land neighbour.San Marino: Entirely surrounded by Italy, it is a microstate whose only neighbour is Italy.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Gambia: A narrow country surrounded on three sides by Senegal, with the Gambia River running through its middle.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Qatar: Its only land border is with Saudi Arabia, though the rest is surrounded by the Persian Gulf.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Haiti: It shares the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic, its only neighbour.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Brunei: Its land border is only with Malaysia, which splits Brunei into two separate parts.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Papua New Guinea: It shares its only land border with Indonesia, on the island of New Guinea.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Dominican Republic: It shares the island of Hispaniola, and its only border, with Haiti.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Spain: It borders Portugal, France, Andorra and Morocco, plus Gibraltar, so it has several neighbours.

Countries with just one land neighbour.Netherlands: It has two neighbours, Germany and Belgium.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Austria: It borders eight countries, so it is among the most connected in Europe.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Switzerland: It is surrounded by five neighbours, France, Germany, Austria, Liechtenstein and Italy.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Norway: It borders Sweden, Finland and Russia, so it has three neighbours.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Chile: It borders Peru, Bolivia and Argentina, so it has three neighbours.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Uruguay: It has two neighbours, Brazil and Argentina.
Countries with just one land neighbour.Sweden: It borders Norway and Finland, so it has two neighbours.

Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Havana: Cuba's capital keeps thousands of 1950s American cars running on improvised parts, a rolling museum shaped by decades of embargo.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Kingston: Jamaica's capital took over from Spanish Town in 1872 and holds the Bob Marley Museum, set in the reggae star's former home and studio.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.San José: Costa Rica scrapped its army in 1948, and its capital sits in a high valley where spring-like weather lasts nearly all year.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Panama City: The only capital with a rainforest park inside city limits, it also sits at the Pacific mouth of the Panama Canal.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Managua: Nicaragua's capital has no true downtown since the 1972 earthquake flattened its center; it spreads along the shore of Lake Managua.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Tegucigalpa: Honduras's capital began as a silver-mining town; its name is often said to come from a Nahuatl phrase meaning 'silver hill'.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.San Salvador: It lies in the shadow of a volcano that shares its name, and El Salvador is the only Central American country with no Caribbean coast.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Guatemala City: The largest city in Central America, home to roughly a million people, with many more in the surrounding metropolitan area.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Belmopan: Built inland after Hurricane Hattie wrecked Belize City in 1961, it became the capital in 1970 and remains one of the world's smallest.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Santo Domingo: Founded in 1496, it is the oldest permanent European settlement in the Americas, and its Colonial Zone is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Port-au-Prince: Haiti won independence in 1804 after the only successful slave revolt to found a nation, and Port-au-Prince has been its capital since.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Nassau: Capital of the Bahamas, on New Providence island, it was a notorious pirate haven in the early 1700s before the British cleared it out.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Cancún: A trap: Cancún is a Mexican resort built from scratch on a sandbar in the 1970s. Mexico isn't Central America, and its capital is Mexico City.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Belize City: Belize City is the country's largest city, but Hurricane Hattie in 1961 pushed the capital inland to Belmopan.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.León: León is Nicaragua's old colonial rival of Granada; Managua became the capital in 1852 as a compromise between the two feuding cities.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Granada: This colonial gem on Lake Nicaragua feuded with León for centuries, which is partly why neutral Managua was chosen as the capital.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Montego Bay: Jamaica's tourism hub, with a major airport and the resort strip, is a big city, but Kingston remains the capital.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Acapulco: Famous for cliff divers who leap from La Quebrada, Acapulco is a Mexican Pacific resort, so it fits neither Central America nor capital status.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Punta Cana: The Dominican Republic's resort coast has an airport with thatched-roof terminals, but the capital is Santo Domingo, a few hours away.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Varadero: Cuba's best-known beach resort stretches along a narrow peninsula about 20 kilometers long, yet Havana is the capital.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Antigua Guatemala: Antigua was Guatemala's capital until earthquakes in 1773 forced a move, so it is a former capital, and its ruins still draw visitors.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Colón: At the Caribbean entrance to the Panama Canal, Colón is a port and free-trade zone, but Panama City holds the capital title.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.San Pedro Sula: Honduras's industrial and business hub often outshines Tegucigalpa economically, but it is not the capital.
Capitals in Central America and the Cari.Santiago de Cuba: Cuba's second city was once the colonial capital before Havana took over, and it is a cradle of Cuban music, but it isn't today's capital.

Elements named after celestial bodies.Mercury: Named after the planet, itself named for the swift Roman messenger god. The metal's alternative name, quicksilver, means living silver.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Uranium: Named for Uranus, discovered just eight years before the element in 1789. It was Martin Klaproth who honored the new planet.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Neptunium: Named after Neptune and made in 1940, it was the first element found beyond uranium on the periodic table.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Plutonium: Named after Pluto, which was then still a planet, it follows neptunium just as Pluto follows Neptune in the solar system.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Helium: Its name comes from Greek Helios, the Sun. It was found in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 before anyone found it on Earth.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Selenium: Named for Selene, the Greek Moon goddess. It was named because it was found alongside tellurium, whose name means Earth.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Tellurium: Named from Latin tellus, meaning Earth, a planet. A related element, selenium, was named for the Moon in contrast.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Cerium: Named for Ceres, the first asteroid discovered, in 1801, now a dwarf planet. The element appeared two years later.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Palladium: Named for Pallas, the second asteroid found, in 1802. It is now worth more than gold at times, used in car catalytic converters.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Iron: A trap: Iron comes from an old English word, not a celestial body. Meteorites are rich in it, though.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Gold: A trap: it is not named for any celestial body, though ancient alchemists tied gold to the Sun. Its symbol Au comes from Latin aurum.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Neon: A trap: it does not hide its name's roots. Neon's symbol is Ne, and it was named from Greek neos, new, when found in 1898.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Argon: A trap: from Greek argos, meaning lazy or inactive, because it barely reacts. It's not named for a celestial body.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Lithium: A trap: from Greek lithos, meaning stone. It is not named for the heavens, though it powers phone batteries here on Earth.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Silver: A trap: ancient alchemists tied silver to the Moon, but the element's name has no celestial origin.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Carbon: A trap: from Latin carbo, charcoal, not a celestial body. It is created inside stars, though, through fusion.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Cobalt: A trap: named from German Kobold, a mischievous goblin, because miners blamed the ore for poisoning them. Not a celestial body.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Nickel: A trap: from German Nickel, a trickster sprite, not a celestial body. Miners had mistaken its ore for copper.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Americium: A trap: named for the Americas, not a heavenly body. It sits in many household smoke detectors.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Francium: A trap: named for France. It is one of the rarest natural elements and decays within minutes.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Polonium: A trap: named for Poland, not the sky. Marie Curie chose the name to draw attention to her partitioned homeland.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Einsteinium: A trap: named for the physicist Albert Einstein, not a celestial body, though it was first found in a hydrogen bomb's debris.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Curium: A trap: it honors Marie and Pierre Curie, not any celestial object. Both Curies shared a Nobel Prize.
Elements named after celestial bodies.Oxygen: A trap: its name means acid-former, from Greek. Nothing celestial, but stars forge it through fusion.

Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Aslan: The great lion is Narnia's creator and a Christ-like figure. Lewis named him with the Turkish word for 'lion'.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Lucy Pevensie: The youngest Pevensie is the first to find Narnia through the wardrobe, and her siblings only believe her later.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Edmund: He betrays his siblings for Turkish delight in the first book, and is later forgiven and crowned 'King Edmund the Just'.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Peter Pevensie: The eldest sibling, crowned High King of Narnia, wields the sword Rhindon. The Pevensies were evacuated from London in World War II.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Susan: The Pevensie who receives a bow and a horn, and who in the final book is left behind. This fate still sparks much debate among readers.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Mr. Tumnus: The faun who befriends Lucy by a lamppost. Lewis said the whole Narnia series started from an image of a faun carrying an umbrella and parcels.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.White Witch: Jadis rules a Narnia where it is always winter but never Christmas. Her backstory as a ruler of the dead world Charn comes in The Magician's Nephew.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Prince Caspian: The heir to Narnia's throne, who blows Susan's magic horn to summon help. In the story the Pevensies return after 1,300 Narnian years.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Reepicheep: A tiny, brave talking mouse who fights with a rapier. In The Voyage of the Dawn Treader he sails on to the world's end.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Eustace: A whiny cousin whose book opens: 'There was a boy called Eustace Clarence Scrubb, and he almost deserved it.' He turns into a dragon.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Mr. Beaver: One of the first Narnians the children meet. He and Mrs. Beaver shelter them and lead them to Aslan.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Trumpkin: A gruff dwarf who is first doubtful about Aslan and who becomes a faithful ally of Prince Caspian.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Gandalf: The wizard is from Tolkien's Middle-earth. Tolkien was a friend of Lewis, and he read Narnia drafts but didn't care for them.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Frodo: Tolkien's hobbit hero is from Middle-earth. The Inklings, including Tolkien and Lewis, met in an Oxford pub to read their works aloud.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Dobby: The house-elf is from Harry Potter, where he is freed with a sock. J. K. Rowling's world is far from Narnia.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Hagrid: Hogwarts' half-giant gamekeeper belongs to Harry Potter, where he took Harry from his burning home and delivered his letter.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Alice: Alice belongs to Lewis Carroll's Wonderland. Narnia's author is C. S. Lewis, and the near-identical names are only a coincidence.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Mad Hatter: Carroll's tea-party host lives in Wonderland rather than Narnia, though both tales begin with a child passing into a magical other world.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Glinda: Glinda the Good Witch is from Oz, where in the 1939 film she floats in a bubble. Narnia's witch is the villain, not a helper.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Dorothy: Oz's Dorothy was created by L. Frank Baum in 1900, about half a century before Narnia, and no cross-over exists.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Merlin: The wizard of Arthurian legend is not a Narnian, though Lewis did bring Merlin into his adult sci-fi novel That Hideous Strength.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Gollum: The ring-obsessed creature belongs to Tolkien's Middle-earth. Tolkien and Lewis were close friends in the Oxford group The Inklings.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Bilbo: Bilbo Baggins, the hobbit of Tolkien's The Hobbit, lives in Middle-earth, not Narnia, even though both authors were Oxford friends.
Characters in The Chronicles of Narnia.Smaug: The dragon of The Hobbit guards the treasure of the Lonely Mountain. Narnia has dragons too, but Smaug is Tolkien's.

Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Violin: A full orchestra may have around 30 violins, split into firsts and seconds. They carry most of the melody.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Viola: Slightly bigger than a violin and tuned a fifth lower, it reads in its own clef and is the butt of many orchestra jokes.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Cello: Held between the knees and supported by an endpin, it inspired Bach's six unaccompanied suites, a pillar of the repertoire.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Double bass: The biggest string instrument, taller than most children. It keeps the sloping shoulders of the older viol family.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Flute: It is metal yet counts as woodwind, because the sound comes from air splitting over an edge, not from brass lips.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Oboe: The whole orchestra tunes to the oboe's A before a concert, because its pitch is steady and cuts through.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Clarinet: A young instrument, invented around 1700, and Mozart wrote a beloved concerto for it near the end of his life.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Bassoon: Its folded wooden tube is about 2.5 metres long, which would stretch far if straightened out.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.French horn: Despite the name it is German in origin, and its coiled tubing would stretch around 3.5 metres if unwound.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Trumpet: Trumpets of silver and bronze were found in Tutankhamun's tomb, so this horn is thousands of years old.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Trombone: The only common orchestral brass with a slide. Its name means big trumpet in Italian.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Tuba: The deepest brass instrument, invented in Berlin around 1835.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Timpani: Kettledrums tuned to exact pitches using pedals, so they can play melodies as well as rhythms.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Harp: A concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals that change the pitch.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Electric guitar: It is rarely in a standard symphony orchestra, though some modern scores add one, and it needs an amplifier.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Banjo: Descended from West African instruments brought by enslaved people, it grew into an American folk and bluegrass sound, not an orchestral one.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Ukulele: The name is often said to mean jumping flea in Hawaiian. A Hawaiian favourite, not an orchestra member.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Bagpipes: Highland pipes are loud outdoors, so orchestras seldom include them, though a few modern scores do.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Accordion: A free-reed instrument patented in Vienna in 1829, belonging to folk and tango bands more than symphonies.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Harmonica: Vaughan Williams wrote a Romance for harmonica and orchestra, but it is a rare soloist, not a section member.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Sitar: Ravi Shankar brought it to Western ears, and George Harrison played one on Norwegian Wood. It belongs to Indian classical music.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Kazoo: Its buzzing membrane turns humming into sound. Orchestras leave it to jug bands and novelty acts.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Didgeridoo: Made from hollowed eucalyptus branches in Aboriginal Australia, it is one of the oldest wind instruments.
Instruments in a symphony orchestra.Steel drum: Born in Trinidad in the 1930s and 40s, from discarded oil barrels.

Country music singers.Dolly Parton: She wrote Jolene and I Will Always Love You on the same day, according to her own account, and she funds children's books through her Imagination Library.
Country music singers.Johnny Cash: The Man in Black recorded a live album at Folsom Prison in 1968, which revived his career.
Country music singers.Willie Nelson: His battered guitar Trigger is worn through with a hole from decades of play, and has been with him since the 1960s.
Country music singers.Garth Brooks: One of the best-selling solo artists in US history, he is famous for The Dance and his stadium-sized concerts.
Country music singers.Shania Twain: The Canadian's Come On Over is among the best-selling albums ever, and she mixed country with pop in a way that crossed borders.
Country music singers.Kenny Rogers: The Gambler was his signature hit, and he later founded a chicken restaurant chain.
Country music singers.Reba McEntire: The Oklahoma redhead starred in a sitcom named after herself, and she is a country queen with many number-one hits.
Country music singers.Tim McGraw: His father was baseball pitcher Tug McGraw, and he is married to singer Faith Hill.
Country music singers.Carrie Underwood: She won American Idol in 2005, and Before He Cheats turned her into a country superstar.
Country music singers.Patsy Cline: Her Crazy is a jukebox classic, and she died in a plane crash in 1963 at age 30.
Country music singers.Hank Williams: He wrote Your Cheatin' Heart and died aged 29 in 1953, having left behind a huge catalogue.
Country music singers.Blake Shelton: The Voice coach and country star has a number of hits, including Austin and God's Country.
Country music singers.Luke Combs: His Hurricane made him a star, and his 2023 cover of Fast Car, a Tracy Chapman song, became a huge crossover hit.
Country music singers.Bob Marley: The Jamaican reggae star, famous for One Love and Redemption Song, is not a country singer.
Country music singers.Frank Sinatra: The crooner known for My Way sang big-band and pop standards, not country.
Country music singers.Whitney Houston: A trap. Her I Will Always Love You is a Dolly Parton song, so the cover is huge, but she is a pop and R&B diva.
Country music singers.Celine Dion: The Canadian pop diva with a huge voice is best known for My Heart Will Go On, not country.
Country music singers.Adele: The British soul and pop singer won many Grammys, and she is not country.
Country music singers.Bruce Springsteen: The Boss is a rock singer, though his Nebraska album has a folk and country twang.
Country music singers.Billy Joel: The Piano Man plays piano and writes pop and rock ballads, not country.
Country music singers.Stevie Wonder: The Motown legend, blind since birth, is a soul and pop star who also wrote Isn't She Lovely.
Country music singers.Eminem: The Detroit rapper's Lose Yourself won an Oscar, but his genre is hip hop, not country.
Country music singers.Lady Gaga: The pop star's Shallow with Bradley Cooper has a country flavour, and she tried country-rock on Joanne, but she is pop.
Country music singers.Ozzy Osbourne: Black Sabbath's singer, known as the Prince of Darkness, is a heavy metal icon, not country.

Led Zeppelin songs.Stairway to Heaven: Led Zeppelin never released it as a US single, yet it became one of the most-played songs in rock radio history; Jimmy Page's guitar builds across eight minutes.
Led Zeppelin songs.Whole Lotta Love: Page's theremin whooshes in the middle, and Willie Dixon later won a credit after a lawsuit over his song You Need Love.
Led Zeppelin songs.Kashmir: Robert Plant said it was inspired by a long drive through the Moroccan desert, not by the actual Kashmir region.
Led Zeppelin songs.Black Dog: Named after a Labrador that wandered into the studio; John Paul Jones wrote the stop-start riff, which is built to confuse people trying to clap along.
Led Zeppelin songs.Immigrant Song: Written after a 1970 trip to Iceland, with Viking war cries; it got a second life in Thor: Ragnarok.
Led Zeppelin songs.Dazed and Confused: Page borrowed the song from Jake Holmes, and plays the guitar with a violin bow during the creepy middle section.
Led Zeppelin songs.Ramble On: Plant's lyrics name Gollum and Mordor, one of several Tolkien nods in Zeppelin's songs.
Led Zeppelin songs.Good Times Bad Times: The opening track of their 1969 debut; John Bonham's fast kick-drum triplets are played with a single bass drum pedal.
Led Zeppelin songs.Going to California: A soft acoustic track from Led Zeppelin IV, thought to be a tribute to Joni Mitchell and her folk scene in California.
Led Zeppelin songs.Trampled Under Foot: A Physical Graffiti funk groove inspired by Stevie Wonder's Superstition, with John Paul Jones on clavinet.
Led Zeppelin songs.Smoke on the Water: Deep Purple, 1972. It tells of a casino fire in Montreux, Switzerland, during a Frank Zappa concert; the riff is rock's most famous but not Zeppelin's.
Led Zeppelin songs.Highway to Hell: AC/DC, 1979, the last album with singer Bon Scott; Australian hard rock, not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Paranoid: Black Sabbath, 1970, reportedly written as a quick filler for the album; Ozzy's band, not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Iron Man: Black Sabbath's 1970 song, with Tony Iommi's slow, heavy riff, the building block for metal; not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Purple Haze: Jimi Hendrix, 1967; Hendrix was a rival of Page, but this one isn't Zeppelin's.
Led Zeppelin songs.Layla: Derek and the Dominos, with Eric Clapton writing about his love for Pattie Boyd; the piano coda was by Jim Gordon.
Led Zeppelin songs.Free Bird: Lynyrd Skynyrd's ballad ends with an epic solo, and fans still shout its name at unrelated concerts; not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Hotel California: The Eagles, 1976. Zeppelin's Going to California shares a state, but this is a different band.
Led Zeppelin songs.Bohemian Rhapsody: Queen, 1975. It's six minutes of ballad, opera, and rock that was released as a single anyway; not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Back in Black: AC/DC's 1980 album, a tribute to Bon Scott, is one of the best-selling albums ever; it isn't Zeppelin's.
Led Zeppelin songs.Sweet Child o' Mine: Guns N' Roses, 1987. Slash's famous riff began as a warm-up exercise, but it's not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Born to Be Wild: Steppenwolf, 1968. Its line about heavy metal thunder is often credited with popularizing the term; it's not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Comfortably Numb: Pink Floyd, from The Wall; David Gilmour's solo is a classic, but it's Pink Floyd, not Zeppelin.
Led Zeppelin songs.Black Magic Woman: Originally Fleetwood Mac's song by Peter Green, made famous by Santana; it's the blues-rock, not Zeppelin.

Sports movies.Rocky: The 1976 film, written by and starring Sylvester Stallone, won the Best Picture Oscar and made the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps famous.
Sports movies.Rudy: Based on the true story of Rudy Ruettiger, who played just one play at Notre Dame; the real ending shows the team carrying him off.
Sports movies.Hoosiers: The 1986 basketball film is loosely based on tiny Milan High School winning the 1954 Indiana state title.
Sports movies.Space Jam: 1996's mix of live action and cartoon features Michael Jordan and the Looney Tunes, and its website has stayed online for decades.
Sports movies.Remember the Titans: Denzel Washington plays Herman Boone, coach of a newly integrated Virginia high school football team in 1971.
Sports movies.Moneyball: Brad Pitt plays Oakland's Billy Beane, who used statistics to build a winning baseball team on a small budget in 2002.
Sports movies.Cool Runnings: A comedy loosely inspired by Jamaica's first Olympic bobsled team at the 1988 Calgary Games, though many details were invented.
Sports movies.The Mighty Ducks: This 1992 film about a misfit youth hockey team inspired Disney to found a real NHL team of the same name.
Sports movies.Raging Bull: Martin Scorsese's black-and-white 1980 boxing biopic of Jake LaMotta, for which Robert De Niro gained about 60 pounds.
Sports movies.Caddyshack: A 1980 golf comedy with Bill Murray, Chevy Chase and a mechanical gopher, and set at a snooty country club.
Sports movies.Field of Dreams: 1989's baseball fantasy was shot on a real Iowa farm, and the field still draws visitors; its famous line was 'If you build it, he will come.'
Sports movies.Seabiscuit: A film about an undersized racehorse who became a Depression-era hero, and beat War Admiral in a famed 1938 match race.
Sports movies.Chariots of Fire: The 1981 film about British runners at the 1924 Olympics won Best Picture and has one of the most recognisable synth themes.
Sports movies.Jaws: A shark thriller, but not about sport: its 1975 release is credited with creating the summer blockbuster.
Sports movies.Titanic: A romance on a doomed liner, whose 1997 release won 11 Oscars, with no sports.
Sports movies.Grease: A 1978 musical about high school, with a dance contest but not really a sports film.
Sports movies.Toy Story: The first fully computer-animated feature, in 1995, about living toys, not a sports tale.
Sports movies.The Godfather: Francis Ford Coppola's 1972 crime saga has no sports plot.
Sports movies.Casablanca: A 1942 wartime romance, which, despite its status as a classic, has no sports.
Sports movies.Frozen: A Disney animation about snow and ice, but not about winter sports.
Sports movies.Inception: A dream-heist film from 2010; its spinning top is not sports equipment.
Sports movies.Shrek: A 2001 animated fairy-tale comedy, with no sporting theme.
Sports movies.Top Gun: A fighter-pilot film with a famous beach volleyball scene, but its subject is the Navy, not sport.
Sports movies.Gladiator: Ancient Rome's arena combat was spectacle and bloodsport, but the 2000 film is a historical epic, not a sports movie.

Races run on foot.Sprint: The 100 m is the classic. Usain Bolt's 9.58 seconds, set in 2009, is still the world record.
Races run on foot.Relay: Four runners pass a baton, and dropped or late handoffs are the classic way a relay team loses.
Races run on foot.Marathon: Its 26.2-mile distance was fixed after the 1908 London Olympics, reportedly so the race could start at Windsor Castle.
Races run on foot.Hurdles: Modern hurdles tip over when hit, but knocking one still costs speed and rhythm. In the 400 m, runners clear ten.
Races run on foot.Steeplechase: Named for old horse races toward a church steeple. The 3,000 m version has 28 barriers and seven water jumps.
Races run on foot.Cross country: Run over mud, grass and hills, and international championships go back to 1903.
Races run on foot.Ultramarathon: Anything longer than a marathon. The Western States 100, a famous 100-mile trail race, gives runners 30 hours to finish.
Races run on foot.Half marathon: At 13.1 miles it's exactly half a marathon, and top men finish in under an hour.
Races run on foot.Egg-and-spoon race: A sports-day staple where dropping the egg means stopping to pick it up. Potato stand-ins are common for a spud-and-spoon twist.
Races run on foot.Sack race: Runners hop with both feet in a sack. Short, quick hops beat big leaps, which tend to end in a fall.
Races run on foot.Three-legged race: Two runners tie adjacent legs together. Teams do best by starting with the tied legs and calling out the step.
Races run on foot.Fun run: Mostly untimed and about taking part. San Francisco's Bay to Breakers is a famous costumed one.
Races run on foot.Grand Prix: Motor racing's top level, from French for big prize. The first was held in France in 1906.
Races run on foot.Regatta: Boat racing. The word regatta comes from Italian and first described gondola races in Venice.
Races run on foot.Rally: Cars race against the clock on public roads or stages. The Monte Carlo Rally has run since 1911.
Races run on foot.Drag race: Cars launch from a standstill down a straight. Top Fuel dragsters cover 1,000 feet in under four seconds.
Races run on foot.Boat race: Rowing, not running. Oxford has faced Cambridge on the Thames since 1829.
Races run on foot.Tour de France: This is cycling, held since 1903 over about three weeks.
Races run on foot.Iditarod: Sled dogs run this roughly 1,000-mile Alaskan race, honouring the 1925 diphtheria serum run to Nome.
Races run on foot.Le Mans: A 24-hour car race in France, held since 1923. Cars do the running.
Races run on foot.Soapbox derby: Gravity-powered homemade cars. The All-American Soap Box Derby has run in Akron since 1934.
Races run on foot.Kentucky Derby: Horses run a mile and a quarter. It has been run every year since 1875.
Races run on foot.Bobsleigh: A sled on an ice track. The name comes from early riders bobbing back and forth to gain speed.
Races run on foot.Keirin: It sounds like a footrace, but it's a Japanese cycling sprint behind a pacing motorbike.

Pharaohs of Egypt.Tutankhamun: The boy king who died at about 18. His tomb, found nearly intact in 1922 by Howard Carter, held over 5,000 objects.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Ramses II: Ruled for about 66 years, built Abu Simbel and fathered, it's said, over 100 children. He's often called Ramses the Great.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Cleopatra: Egypt's last active pharaoh, she was actually of Greek Macedonian descent, and is said to have been the first in her dynasty to learn Egyptian.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Khufu: Builder of the Great Pyramid of Giza, the only surviving wonder of the ancient world. A tiny ivory figurine is nearly all we have of his likeness.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Hatshepsut: One of Egypt's few female pharaohs, she ruled for about 20 years and was shown wearing a ceremonial false beard.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Akhenaten: He tried to make Egypt worship just one god, the sun disk Aten, and moved the capital. After his death, his reforms were reversed.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Thutmose III: A warrior pharaoh who led about 17 campaigns and has been called Egypt's Napoleon. He ruled for over 50 years.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Seti I: Father of Ramses II, his tomb in the Valley of the Kings is the longest and deepest there, and covered in painted reliefs.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Djoser: His architect, Imhotep, built the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first major stone building in Egypt around 2650 BC.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Khafre: Builder of the second Giza pyramid and probably the Sphinx, whose face may be modeled after his own.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Menkaure: Builder of the smallest of the three Giza pyramids, with a pink granite lower casing. His reign is the last of that trio.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Imhotep: A trap: he was no pharaoh but Djoser's architect and a physician-priest. He was later worshipped as a god of medicine.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Howard Carter: The British archaeologist who discovered Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922. He found a pharaoh's treasures, but wasn't one.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Hannibal: A Carthaginian general who marched war elephants across the Alps to attack Rome. Carthage was in North Africa, not Egypt.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Leonidas: The Spartan king who led the famous stand of 300 at Thermopylae in 480 BC. Greek, not Egyptian.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Pericles: The Athenian statesman who oversaw the building of the Parthenon during Athens' golden age.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Nebuchadnezzar: The Babylonian king said to have built the Hanging Gardens, and who conquered Jerusalem in 587 BC.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Hammurabi: A Babylonian king known for one of the oldest law codes, carved on a stone pillar nearly 3,800 years ago.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Cyrus the Great: The founder of the Persian Empire, famous for freeing the Jews from Babylon. He conquered, but not Egypt, which his son Cambyses took.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Herod: The Roman-era king of Judea, who rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem. He ruled a client state, not Egypt.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Ashoka: An Indian emperor of the Maurya dynasty who embraced Buddhism and spread it across Asia after a bloody war.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Attila: The king of the Huns, called the "Scourge of God," who terrorized the Roman Empire in the 400s AD.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Saladin: The Muslim sultan who retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187. He did rule Egypt, but as a sultan, not a pharaoh.
Pharaohs of Egypt.Gilgamesh: A legendary king of Uruk in Mesopotamia and hero of an epic from about 4,000 years ago, not an Egyptian pharaoh.

From Slavic folklore.Baba Yaga: A witch who flies in a mortar and lives in a hut that stands on chicken legs; she can be either helper or devourer.
From Slavic folklore.Koschei: The 'Deathless' villain hides his soul in a needle inside an egg, inside a duck, inside a hare, inside a chest.
From Slavic folklore.Firebird: A glowing bird whose feather brings luck and danger; Stravinsky's 1910 ballet made it famous worldwide.
From Slavic folklore.Perun: The Slavic thunder god, associated with oaks, who was worshipped in Kyiv before Christianity arrived in 988.
From Slavic folklore.Rusalka: The spirit of a drowned young woman who lures men into water; Dvorak's opera about one premiered in 1901.
From Slavic folklore.Domovoi: A household spirit living behind the stove; families would leave out bread or porridge and say hello to keep him friendly.
From Slavic folklore.Leshy: The forest guardian, who can change his size, and leads travelers astray; they could break the spell by wearing clothes backwards.
From Slavic folklore.Vodyanoy: A grumpy water spirit with a fish tail and a beard of weed, who is said to drown people and break mill dams.
From Slavic folklore.Zmey Gorynych: A three-headed, fire-breathing dragon of Russian epics, who is slain by the hero Dobrynya Nikitich.
From Slavic folklore.Veles: A Slavic god of cattle, magic and the underworld, and Perun's rival in a myth where Perun chases him around.
From Slavic folklore.Kikimora: A house spirit who spins at night; if she is unhappy, she tangles the yarn and makes noise.
From Slavic folklore.Banshee: A trap: this wailing spirit, a harbinger of death, is Irish and not Slavic, and its Irish name means 'woman of the fairy mound'.
From Slavic folklore.Leprechaun: A trap: the Irish shoemaker fairy guards a pot of gold and belongs to Irish folklore, not Slavic.
From Slavic folklore.Troll: A trap: Scandinavian trolls turn to stone in sunlight, in Nordic folklore rather than Slavic.
From Slavic folklore.Valkyrie: A trap: Odin's Norse battle maidens, who carry slain warriors to Valhalla, are not Slavic.
From Slavic folklore.Kitsune: A trap: Japanese fox spirits grow more tails with age, up to nine, and belong to Japan, not Slavic lands.
From Slavic folklore.Djinn: A trap: Arabian spirits made of smokeless fire, from Islamic and pre-Islamic Arabian lore, not Slavic.
From Slavic folklore.Wendigo: A trap: a cannibal spirit from Algonquian tales in North America, not Slavic.
From Slavic folklore.Chupacabra: A trap: this 'goat-sucker' was first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995, so it's modern, not old Slavic folklore.
From Slavic folklore.Selkie: A trap: seal-people who shed their skins are from Scottish and Irish folklore, not Slavic.
From Slavic folklore.Kelpie: A trap: this shape-shifting water horse that drowns riders comes from Scottish folklore.
From Slavic folklore.Tengu: A trap: the beaked mountain goblin of Japan has nothing to do with Slavic folklore.
From Slavic folklore.Krampus: A trap: the horned Christmas beast that punishes bad children is Alpine, from Austria and Bavaria.
From Slavic folklore.Pixie: A trap: these small fairies come from folklore in southwest England, in Devon and Cornwall.

Ancient Chinese inventions.Paper: Traditionally credited to Cai Lun in AD 105, though paper fragments are older. It spread west along the Silk Road and reached Europe about 1,000 years later.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Gunpowder: Probably found by Chinese alchemists seeking an elixir of life around the 9th century. Ironically it was one of history's deadliest finds.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Magnetic compass: Chinese people first used lodestone spoons for divination and feng shui, then for navigation by around the 11th century.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Silk: According to legend, Empress Leizu discovered silk when a cocoon dropped in her tea. China guarded the secret of silk-making for thousands of years.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Porcelain: Perfected in China under the Tang and later dynasties, using kaolin clay fired at high temperatures. Europe did not copy it until about 1708.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Kite: Chinese kites were used for signalling, measuring distance and even in military trials over 2,000 years ago. They later inspired aviation experiments.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Seismograph: Zhang Heng built one in AD 132. A bronze vessel with eight dragon heads dropped a ball into a toad's mouth to show an earthquake's direction.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Paper money: Invented in Song China around the 11th century, after merchants found coins too heavy. Marco Polo was amazed by it.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Fireworks: They began as bamboo stems thrown into fire, which explode with a bang to scare off evil spirits. Later gunpowder made them colourful.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Chopsticks: Used in China for more than 3,000 years, and first just as cooking sticks. Over time they spread across East Asia.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Woodblock printing: Printing from carved wooden blocks began in China before AD 868, when the Diamond Sutra was printed. It predates Gutenberg by centuries.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Telescope: A Dutch spectacle-maker patented it in 1608, and Galileo improved it. It was not a Chinese invention.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Steam engine: Developed in Europe, beginning with Newcomen in 1712. It is not an ancient Chinese invention.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Light bulb: Edison's and Swan's practical bulbs came in the late 1870s. Chinese inventors of the period were not in the story.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell patented it in 1876. It is a late 19th-century invention.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Airplane: The Wright brothers flew in 1903 in the US. China did have kites and early rockets, but not powered flight.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Concrete: Roman builders perfected concrete, using volcanic ash. It is a trap, as the Romans, not the Chinese, are the ancient masters of it.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Aqueduct: Associated with the Romans, though Persians and others built channels earlier. It is not a famous Chinese invention.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Alphabet: Created by Semitic peoples in the Near East by about 1800 BC. Chinese writing uses characters instead.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Wheel: Appeared in Mesopotamia around 3500 BC. China adopted it later, so this is not a Chinese invention.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Pencil: Graphite pencils arose in England after a 1564 discovery of graphite in Borrowdale. It is not Chinese.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Thermometer: Galileo and others developed early versions around 1600 in Europe. Fahrenheit built the mercury kind in 1714.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Microscope: Made in the Netherlands around 1600. Leeuwenhoek later used it to see bacteria in the 1670s.
Ancient Chinese inventions.Piano: Invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Italy around 1700. A European instrument, not Chinese.

Alive at some point in the 1800s.Abraham Lincoln: Born in 1809, he led the United States through the Civil War until his assassination in 1865.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Queen Victoria: She ruled from 1837 to 1901, and the British era of her name took in the whole century nearly.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Charles Dickens: His novels appeared in serial installments, and his readers waited for each instalment of Oliver Twist.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Charles Darwin: His On the Origin of Species came out in 1859 and sold out on its first day.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Florence Nightingale: Crimean War nurse, and a pioneer in statistics, inventing a form of pie chart.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Van Gogh: He lived 1853 to 1890 and painted around 2,000 works, but sold very few while alive.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Napoleon: Born in 1769 and died in 1821, so the 1800s counted: he crowned himself emperor in 1804.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Beethoven: Born 1770 and died 1827, so he lived 27 years of the 1800s and wrote his Ninth Symphony while deaf.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Jane Austen: She lived 1775 to 1817, and her novels were all published between 1811 and 1818.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Mark Twain: Born 1835 when Halley's Comet appeared, he died in 1910 when it returned, as he predicted.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Tchaikovsky: He lived 1840 to 1893 and wrote Swan Lake and the Nutcracker.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Harriet Tubman: Having escaped slavery in 1849, she led about 70 people to freedom through the Underground Railroad.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Louis Pasteur: His 1800s work gave us pasteurization and a rabies vaccine in 1885.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Shakespeare: He died in 1616, nearly two centuries before the 1800s even began, so his life never touched them.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Isaac Newton: He died in 1727, nearly 75 years before the 1800s, after formulating gravity and calculus in the 1600s.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Mozart: Mozart died in 1791 at age 35, just nine years before the 1800s began.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.George Washington: The first US president died on December 14, 1799, a few weeks short of the new century.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Benjamin Franklin: He died in 1790, a full decade before the 1800s, after helping to write the Declaration of Independence.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Elvis Presley: The King of Rock and Roll was born in 1935 and died in 1977, a 1900s star.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Leonardo da Vinci: He died in 1519, about 300 years before the 1800s, leaving behind the Mona Lisa and thousands of notebook pages.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Galileo: He died in 1642, having spent his last years under house arrest, well over a century too early.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Henry VIII: Henry VIII, with his six wives, died in 1547, roughly 250 years before the 1800s began.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Joan of Arc: She was burned at the stake in 1431, nearly four centuries before the 1800s began.
Alive at some point in the 1800s.Neil Armstrong: He was born in 1930 and walked on the Moon in 1969, a 1900s story entirely.

Historic landmarks in France.Eiffel Tower: The 1889 iron tower was meant to be temporary, and nearly torn down in 1909. It now draws millions of visitors yearly.
Historic landmarks in France.Versailles: Louis XIV's enormous palace outside Paris, where the Treaty of Versailles ended World War I in 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors.
Historic landmarks in France.Notre-Dame: The Paris cathedral began in 1163 and took about two centuries. A 2019 fire destroyed its spire, and it reopened in 2024.
Historic landmarks in France.Mont-Saint-Michel: A rocky tidal island topped with an abbey. The sea rushes in fast at high tide, and it becomes an island again.
Historic landmarks in France.Arc de Triomphe: Napoleon ordered it in 1806 to honor his armies. It now shelters the tomb of France's Unknown Soldier from World War I.
Historic landmarks in France.Louvre: It started as a medieval fortress before becoming a palace and then the world's most visited museum, home to the Mona Lisa.
Historic landmarks in France.Pont du Gard: A Roman aqueduct bridge in southern France, about 49 metres high, built around 2,000 years ago without mortar.
Historic landmarks in France.Chambord: The biggest chateau in the Loire Valley, with a famous double-helix staircase often linked to Leonardo da Vinci.
Historic landmarks in France.Carcassonne: A walled medieval city in southern France with 52 towers. Its restoration in the 1800s is still debated by historians.
Historic landmarks in France.Lascaux: A cave in the Dordogne with Paleolithic paintings about 17,000 years old. It was closed to preserve them, and a replica opened nearby.
Historic landmarks in France.Sainte-Chapelle: A Gothic chapel on Paris's Ile de la Cite, built for relics and famous for walls of stained glass.
Historic landmarks in France.Big Ben: Trap: this clock tower stands in London, and 'Big Ben' is actually the nickname of its great bell.
Historic landmarks in France.Colosseum: Trap: Rome's amphitheatre, finished about 80 AD. It could hold tens of thousands of spectators.
Historic landmarks in France.Sagrada Familia: Trap: Gaudi's unfinished basilica in Barcelona. Work began in 1882, and it is still under construction, but it's Spanish, not French.
Historic landmarks in France.Neuschwanstein: Trap: a Bavarian fairytale castle from the 1800s that inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
Historic landmarks in France.Alhambra: Trap: a Moorish palace-fortress in Granada, Spain. Its walls are covered in intricate tilework and Arabic poetry, nothing French.
Historic landmarks in France.Tower of London: Trap: William the Conqueror's fortress in London, a landmark that is English. Its guardians include famous resident ravens.
Historic landmarks in France.Brandenburg Gate: Trap: a Berlin gate finished in 1791, topped with a chariot sculpture. German, and a symbol of reunification in 1989.
Historic landmarks in France.Acropolis: Trap: a temple complex in Athens, topped by the Parthenon, built in the fifth century BC.
Historic landmarks in France.Atomium: Trap: a Brussels landmark, a giant model of an iron crystal built for the 1958 World's Fair. Belgian, not French.
