Cards usually made of plastic.Credit card: Credit cards are standardized at about 85.6 by 54 mm, and the size was set by an international standard so they fit every reader.
Cards usually made of plastic.Debit card: Debit cards are plastic, usually PVC, with a magnetic stripe and chip; they're made in standard thickness of about 0.76 mm.
Cards usually made of plastic.Gift card: Gift cards are plastic and billions go unspent, with many people forgetting a balance of a few dollars forever.
Cards usually made of plastic.Driver's license: Many licenses are plastic polycarbonate, laser-engraved so the photo can't be peeled off or altered without leaving traces.
Cards usually made of plastic.Hotel key card: Hotel key cards carry a magnetic stripe or chip, and the lock reads a code that changes with each new guest.
Cards usually made of plastic.Library card: Library cards are often plastic with a barcode, and a card can open a world of books, movies, and sometimes tools or seeds.
Cards usually made of plastic.Loyalty card: Loyalty cards are small plastic tags that track purchases, and a big use is helping stores learn what customers buy.
Cards usually made of plastic.Gym card: Gym membership cards are plastic and carry a barcode or chip, and about half of gym members rarely use them.
Cards usually made of plastic.Transit card: Many transit cards, like London's Oyster, use contactless chips, and a tap takes less than a second to register.
Cards usually made of plastic.Student ID card: Student IDs are plastic with a photo, and they often unlock discounts, libraries, and doors on campus.
Cards usually made of plastic.SIM card: A SIM card is a tiny plastic card, though only the chip's gold contacts do the work; the plastic is just a carrier.
Cards usually made of plastic.Business card: Business cards are made of paper stock, and in Japan the exchange of them is a formal ritual, often with both hands.
Cards usually made of plastic.Receipt: Receipts are printed on thermal paper, which turns dark when heated and may contain a chemical like BPA.
Cards usually made of plastic.Postcard: A postcard is stiff card stock, and the first official postcards appeared in Austria in 1869.
Cards usually made of plastic.Postage stamp: Stamps are paper with gum on the back, and the world's first adhesive stamp was Britain's 1840 Penny Black.
Cards usually made of plastic.Ticket stub: A ticket stub is paper or card, and it's often saved as a memento long after the concert or movie is over.
Cards usually made of plastic.Coupon: Coupons are paper, and Coca-Cola's early 1888 coupon for a free drink is often called the first big coupon campaign.
Cards usually made of plastic.Bookmark: Bookmarks are usually paper, leather, or metal, and plastic ones aren't the norm, even if the shape is a card.
Cards usually made of plastic.Sticky note: Sticky notes came about by accident at 3M, when Spencer Silver made a glue too weak to stick permanently.
Cards usually made of plastic.Envelope: An envelope is paper, and the first ones appeared around the 1800s; before that people folded letters and sealed them with wax.
Cards usually made of plastic.Greeting card: Greeting cards are paper, and some 6 billion are sold in the US every year, with Christmas the top season.
Cards usually made of plastic.Boarding pass: Boarding passes are paper or digital, and the barcode on them holds your name, flight, and seat details.
Cards usually made of plastic.Recipe card: Recipe cards are printed paper stock so they can survive kitchen splashes, though grease stains tell you a favorite.
Cards usually made of plastic.Index card: Index cards are heavy paper, and the 3 by 5 inch size was popularized by library catalogs and later became a study tool.

Things you feed coins into.Vending machine: Vending machines were first recorded in ancient Egypt, where a coin dropped in gave you holy water, according to Hero of Alexandria.
Things you feed coins into.Parking meter: Parking meters began in Oklahoma City in 1935, and the first one was installed to keep spaces turning over.
Things you feed coins into.Gumball machine: Gumball machines are a staple of shops and stores, and they became popular in the early 1900s.
Things you feed coins into.Jukebox: Jukeboxes let people choose songs for a coin, and their golden age was the 1940s and 50s.
Things you feed coins into.Laundromat washer: Laundromat washers are coin or card fed, and they need exact change in some places.
Things you feed coins into.Payphone: Payphones once ate a coin per call, and in the age of mobile phones they are fast disappearing.
Things you feed coins into.Piggy bank: A piggy bank takes coins on purpose, and the name apparently comes from 'pygg', an old word for clay.
Things you feed coins into.Wishing well: Wishing wells collect coins from people who toss them in with a wish, and the money often goes to charity.
Things you feed coins into.Toll booth: Toll booths take coins in some places, though many roads now use electronic tags instead.
Things you feed coins into.Coin-op arcade game: Coin-op arcade games run on quarters, and the 1970s arcade boom was so big that machines like Space Invaders reportedly caused local coin shortages in Japan.
Things you feed coins into.Smart TV: A smart TV is plugged in and needs no coins to run.
Things you feed coins into.Toaster: A toaster uses electricity from the wall and has no coin slot.
Things you feed coins into.Fridge: A fridge is wired to the mains, so no coin is needed.
Things you feed coins into.ATM: An ATM gives out cash from cards, so it works the opposite way around.
Things you feed coins into.Card reader: A card reader takes a tap or a swipe of plastic, not coins, which is why it appears on the list of things that look like payment slots but aren't.
Things you feed coins into.Laptop: A laptop runs on a battery or charger, and it takes no coins.
Things you feed coins into.Lawnmower: A lawnmower runs on petrol or electricity, with no coin slot.
Things you feed coins into.Kettle: A kettle needs only water and power to boil.
Things you feed coins into.Doorbell: A doorbell is a simple button, and no coin is required.
Things you feed coins into.Treadmill: A treadmill runs on electricity, and gyms don't charge by coin.
Things you feed coins into.Escalator: An escalator runs freely for anyone who steps on.
Things you feed coins into.Dishwasher: A dishwasher at home needs water and power and doesn't take coins.
Things you feed coins into.Microwave: A microwave runs from a power outlet, so the only thing you feed it is food.
Things you feed coins into.Elevator: An elevator takes you for free, apart from in a few odd cases.

Types of cup.Teacup: Teacups had no handles when they first came from China, and Europeans added them to protect fingers from heat.
Types of cup.Mug: A mug is taller and thicker than a cup, and its handle was designed to hold hot drinks safely. Americans love them.
Types of cup.Sippy cup: Sippy cups were designed in the 1980s to stop spills, and speech therapists now say long use can affect mouth development.
Types of cup.Paper cup: The first paper cups were sold in the early 1900s as a germ-free alternative to the shared public cup.
Types of cup.Egg cup: Egg cups hold a boiled egg upright for dipping toast soldiers, a favorite British breakfast ritual.
Types of cup.Measuring cup: A standard US measuring cup is 8 fluid ounces, but a UK cup used to be different, so recipes can mislead.
Types of cup.Espresso cup: Espresso cups are small and thick-walled to keep the shot warm. Their demitasse name means half a cup in French.
Types of cup.Coffee cup: Coffee cups are often thicker than teacups to keep drinks hot, and a coffee cup of the 1700s was often handle-less too.
Types of cup.Plastic cup: Plastic cups are often made of polypropylene, and the recycling number 5 on the bottom identifies it.
Types of cup.Camping cup: Camping cups are often enamel or titanium so they survive being dropped and can even be heated over a campfire.
Types of cup.Cupcake: A cupcake isn't a cup: the name probably refers either to baking in cups or to a recipe measuring by cups.
Types of cup.Cupboard: A cupboard was originally a board for displaying cups. The name stuck as it turned into an enclosed cabinet.
Types of cup.Buttercup: Buttercup flowers have a glossy petal surface that reflects yellow light, which is why chins glow in the old game.
Types of cup.Hiccup: A hiccup is a spasm of the diaphragm followed by the vocal cords snapping shut. The sound is the 'hic'.
Types of cup.Cupid: Cupid is the Roman god of desire, and his name comes from the Latin word for longing. He's the child of Venus.
Types of cup.Teapot: A teapot holds the brew rather than the drink. The first teapots were made from tiny clay Chinese wine pots.
Types of cup.Saucer: A saucer originally held sauces. Later it became the plate under a teacup, and some folks drank tea from it.
Types of cup.Bowl: A bowl is wider and open, with no handle, so it's not a cup. Some Asian tea bowls are the exception.
Types of cup.Jug: A jug is a container with a handle and a lip for pouring, used for serving rather than sipping.
Types of cup.Ladle: Ladles scoop soup from a pot into a bowl, and the word dates to Old English meaning 'to lade' or load.
Types of cup.Vase: A vase holds flowers. Its tall shape does resemble a cup, but it's meant to be seen rather than sipped from.
Types of cup.Pitcher: A pitcher in the US is a jug for liquid. In baseball, it's the player who throws the ball.
Types of cup.Kettle: A kettle heats water, and electric ones can boil a liter in about three minutes.
Types of cup.Gravy boat: A gravy boat is shaped for pouring sauce, with a spout and handle, and is never used as a cup.

Things that existed in ancient Rome.Aqueduct: Roman aqueducts carried water over arches for miles, and some, like the Pont du Gard in France, still stand today.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Chariot: The chariot was Rome's racing vehicle, and the Circus Maximus could seat well over 100,000 fans at its peak.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Toga: A toga was the formal garment of Roman citizens, and it was a long piece of wool draped by hand with no fasteners.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Colosseum: The Colosseum opened in AD 80, held tens of thousands of spectators, and even had a system of trapdoors for staging games.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Sandals: Roman sandals were common for everyday wear, and soldiers wore hobnailed ones called caligae, which gave Caligula his nickname.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Gladiators: Gladiators fought in arenas, and not all died, since their trainers invested heavily in them and many retired.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Public baths: Public baths were the social hub of Roman cities, with hot, warm, and cold rooms and heated floors called hypocausts.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Mosaic: Roman mosaics were made of tiny stones called tesserae, and they decorated floors in homes and baths across the empire.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Olive oil: Olive oil was a Roman staple used for cooking, lamps, and cleaning skin, and athletes scraped it off with a strigil.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Scrolls: Romans wrote on scrolls, and the codex, the book with pages, only slowly took over after about AD 100.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Roman numerals: Roman numerals are still on clocks and Super Bowl logos, and they never had a symbol for zero.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Legionaries: A legion's soldiers were called legionaries, and a legion had about 5,000 men, who also built roads and bridges.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Potato: A trap: the potato came from South America, and Europeans didn't see one until the 1500s, long after Rome.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Tomato: Tomatoes came from the Americas, and Romans never tasted one, since Europe met them after 1492.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Chocolate: Chocolate came from Mesoamerica, where the Maya and Aztecs made cacao drinks, so Romans never tasted any.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Popcorn: Popcorn originates in the Americas, with ancient kernels in Peru over 6,000 years old, so Romans had no popcorn at their games.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Printing press: The printing press was Gutenberg's in about 1440, so Rome's books had to be copied by hand.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Gunpowder: Gunpowder was invented in China, in about the 9th century, so Roman soldiers fought with spears and swords.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Eyeglasses: Eyeglasses appeared in northern Italy in the late 1200s, and Romans only used polished gems or water-filled glass to magnify.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Pizza: A trap: Romans ate flatbreads with toppings, but modern pizza needs tomatoes, and it came to Naples centuries later.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Telescope: The telescope was patented in the Netherlands in 1608, so Roman astronomers watched the sky with the naked eye.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Coffee: Coffee came from Ethiopia and reached Europe in the 1600s, so Romans were drinking wine, not espresso.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Pumpkin: Pumpkins are native to the Americas, so Rome knew gourds, but never the orange pumpkin of Halloween.
Things that existed in ancient Rome.Chili pepper: Chili peppers are from the Americas, so Romans spiced meals with black pepper imported from India instead.

Things that have a lid.Jar: A jar's lid is a classic screw top, and the Mason jar's screw-on lid, patented in 1858, made home canning widespread.
Things that have a lid.Cooking pot: A cooking pot's lid traps steam and heat, which cooks food faster and uses less water and energy.
Things that have a lid.Trash can: A trash can's lid keeps smells and animals in check, and raccoons are clever enough to open many of them.
Things that have a lid.Toilet: A toilet has a lid, and closing it before you flush limits the spray of germs, according to studies.
Things that have a lid.Paint can: A paint can's lid is pried open with a screwdriver, and the lip around the can holds a seal for storage.
Things that have a lid.Teapot: A teapot's lid usually has a tiny hole in it so that the steam can escape and the tea pours smoothly.
Things that have a lid.Eye: An eye has an eyelid, which blinks about 15 to 20 times a minute to spread tears and keep it moist.
Things that have a lid.Blender: A blender's lid is needed to keep contents from flying out, and many have a small cap to add ingredients while running.
Things that have a lid.Kettle: A kettle's lid is often hinged, and many electric kettles shut off by sensing steam at the lid.
Things that have a lid.Shoebox: A shoebox has a lid, and shoeboxes are a classic place for kids to build dioramas.
Things that have a lid.Laptop: A laptop's lid holds the screen, and closing it often puts the computer to sleep through a magnetic sensor.
Things that have a lid.Grand piano: A grand piano has a hinged lid, which can be propped open to project the sound of the strings.
Things that have a lid.Plate: A plate has no lid, though in fancy dining a cloche covers the food, and it's more of a dome.
Things that have a lid.Fork: A fork has tines but no lid, and forks did not become common at European tables until the 1600s.
Things that have a lid.Funnel: A funnel is open at both ends, so it has no lid, and it's made to send liquids into narrow openings.
Things that have a lid.Colander: A colander has holes to drain, so a lid would defeat its purpose.
Things that have a lid.Spatula: A spatula flips and scrapes, and it has no lid, though the name comes from a Latin word for a flat blade.
Things that have a lid.Hula hoop: A hula hoop has no lid, and the toy sold over 25 million in its first months in 1958.
Things that have a lid.Ladder: A ladder has rungs and no lid, and it's one of the oldest tools, depicted in 10,000-year-old cave art.
Things that have a lid.Knife: A knife has a blade but no lid, though some come with a sheath that works as a cover.
Things that have a lid.Straw: A straw has no lid, but a plastic lid with a straw hole is what a to-go cup uses.
Things that have a lid.Chopsticks: Chopsticks are a pair of sticks with no lid, and they've been used for thousands of years.
Things that have a lid.Whisk: A whisk has wires but no lid, and it's made to add air to cream or eggs.
Things that have a lid.Ruler: A ruler has no lid, and the oldest known rulers date from the Indus Valley, about 4,000 years ago.

NATO phonetic alphabet words.Alpha: Alpha is the first Greek letter, and gave us the word alphabet, along with beta.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Bravo: Bravo is Italian for bold, and audiences shout it at the opera and concerts.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Charlie: Charlie stands for C, and the radio code words were chosen to be understandable in many languages.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Delta: Delta is the fourth Greek letter, shaped like a triangle, so a river's fan-shaped mouth is called a delta.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Echo: Echo in Greek myth was a nymph cursed to repeat only the last words spoken to her.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Foxtrot: The foxtrot is a smooth dance from the 1910s, and may be named after the vaudeville performer Harry Fox.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Golf: Golf stands for G, and the sport may come from the Dutch kolf, meaning club.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Hotel: Hotel stands for H, and comes from French hotel, a large townhouse, which gave us hospital.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.India: India stands for I, and the phonetic spelling was set by the ICAO in 1956.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Kilo: Kilo is Greek for thousand, and a kilogram was once defined by a metal cylinder in Paris until 2019.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Lima: Lima is the capital of Peru, and as a code word it stands for L. The spelling, Lee-ma, is set to avoid confusion over radio.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Mike: Mike is the radio word for M. The code words were chosen so each sounds distinct over a crackling line, in many accents.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Oscar: Oscar stands for O, and also names the Academy Awards statuette, a name that appeared in the 1930s.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Tango: Tango is an Argentine dance from Buenos Aires, and stands for T in the alphabet.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Able: Able was the old code for A in the WWII Army-Navy alphabet, which NATO replaced with the new, internationally tested words in 1956.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Baker: Baker was B in the WWII Army-Navy alphabet. Able Baker gave way to Alpha Bravo because the new words suit speakers of many languages.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Dog: Dog stood for D in the WWII alphabet. The words were swapped because many English words don't sound right to non-English speakers.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Easy: Easy was E in the old WWII alphabet, replaced by Echo, and Easy Company of Band of Brothers took its name from it.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Fox: Fox stood for F in the WWII alphabet, and the NATO version lengthened it to Foxtrot, which is a dance, to be clearer on the radio.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.George: George was the old code for G, and Golf took over. Both are plain words, but Golf is easier for speakers of many languages.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.How: How was the old code for H, and it is the odd one out, a question word instead of a name or noun, so Hotel replaced it.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Item: Item was the old code for I, replaced by India. Both the old and new lists were designed to keep letters from being confused on bad lines.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.King: King was the old code for K, and it was swapped for Kilo, a word that sounds the same in many languages.
NATO phonetic alphabet words.Love: Love was the old Army-Navy code for L, used in World War II, and Lima took its place when NATO standardized the alphabet in 1956.

Things a lumberjack uses.Axe: Felling axes cut across the wood grain, unlike splitting mauls, and a sharp one bites rather than bounces.
Things a lumberjack uses.Chainsaw: Kickback can happen when the tip of the bar hits something, so loggers learn to cut with the lower part of the bar.
Things a lumberjack uses.Felling wedge: Tapped into the cut behind the saw, it keeps the blade from pinching and nudges the tree to fall in the planned direction.
Things a lumberjack uses.Peavey: Invented in 1857 by Maine blacksmith Joseph Peavey, its hook and spike let loggers roll heavy logs.
Things a lumberjack uses.Hard hat: Falling branches that loggers call widowmakers make helmets essential.
Things a lumberjack uses.Crosscut saw: A two-person saw pulled alternately in rhythm, nicknamed the misery whip by loggers.
Things a lumberjack uses.Log tongs: Like giant pincers, they grip logs to drag or lift them without ropes.
Things a lumberjack uses.Chainsaw chaps: Layers of fibre inside jam the saw's sprocket if it's cut, stopping the chain.
Things a lumberjack uses.Cant hook: Like a peavey but with a blunt toe instead of a spike; the hook rolls, or cants, logs.
Things a lumberjack uses.Spiked boots: Called caulk boots, with spikes in the sole for grip on slippery logs, as in logrolling contests.
Things a lumberjack uses.Fishing rod: An angler's tool; loggers once floated timber down rivers in big drives, using poles to free jams, but never to fish.
Things a lumberjack uses.Stethoscope: René Laennec's 1816 invention listens to hearts and lungs; a logger tapping a trunk to judge soundness uses an axe handle instead.
Things a lumberjack uses.Whisk: A cook's utensil for beating eggs; loggers' camp cooks fed crews huge breakfasts, but the whisk never goes into the forest.
Things a lumberjack uses.Easel: A painter's stand; the sturdy tools of a logging camp are made for heavy work, not for resting delicate canvases.
Things a lumberjack uses.Thimble: A seamstress's fingertip guard from needlework; a logger's hands rely on thick gloves against splinters and chain.
Things a lumberjack uses.Piping bag: A baker's icing tool; a logger's equivalent of fine decoration is notching a tree trunk so it falls where planned.
Things a lumberjack uses.Gavel: A judge's mallet; the logger's equivalent is a sledgehammer for driving felling wedges deep into the cut.
Things a lumberjack uses.Pinking shears: They cut fabric in a zigzag so edges won't fray; felled timber is cut with saws instead, leaving rough ends.
Things a lumberjack uses.Sextant: A navigator's tool for angles at sea; foresters measure tree heights with a similar angle-based clinometer.
Things a lumberjack uses.Saddle: A horse's seat; horses once dragged logs out of the forest, but they wore harnesses rather than saddles for the job.
Things a lumberjack uses.Baton: A conductor's wand or a relay runner's stick; loggers use a long peavey handle for control instead of any slender stick.
Things a lumberjack uses.Snorkel: A breathing tube for swimmers; loggers who worked river drives balanced on floating logs and tried to stay out of the water.
Things a lumberjack uses.Microscope: Scientists use them; forestry researchers study tree rings under magnification, but loggers read the wood by eye.
Things a lumberjack uses.Paint roller: A decorator's tool; loggers mark trees to cut or keep with spray paint, usually a bright stripe at eye level.

Tools whose names are also verbs.Hammer: To hammer means to pound, and it can also mean to defeat heavily, as in being hammered in a match.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Saw: The tool is also the past tense of see, and sawing with pull strokes, as Japanese saws do, can cut finer than a push.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Drill: Drilling in the military means repeated practice, and the verb for the tool and for training share the same word.
Tools whose names are also verbs.File: A file smooths and shapes metal, and the word is also what you do to papers, but the two meanings came from different roots.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Plane: A hand plane shaves wood thin, and as a verb it means to smooth, though the aircraft sense is a different thing.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Chisel: As a verb it can mean to cheat someone, as in chiseling money out of them.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Rake: The verb means to gather or scratch, and a rake is also a type of dissolute man of old.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Hoe: The hoe is a basic farm tool, and as a verb it means to weed and loosen soil.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Mop: A tool for floors and also the act of cleaning them, and mop can also mean a messy head of hair.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Shovel: You shovel snow and food alike, and shoveling coal powered many a steam engine.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Whisk: A whisk beats air into eggs and cream, and the verb can also mean to move away quickly.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Wrench: As a verb it means to twist violently, and it can also mean a painful emotional pull.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Screwdriver: It is also a cocktail, but the tool can't be used as a verb, since nobody says they screwdriver a screw.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Pliers: The name is plural and can't be used as a verb: you can't say you plier something.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Spanner: It's the British word for wrench, and "spanner in the works" is a saying, but to spanner isn't a verb.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Tweezers: The word is used only as a noun, and you don't tweezer something.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Tape measure: It can't be a verb, as the phrase is just for the tool, though you can measure with it.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Toolbox: It's a noun only, and to toolbox is not a verb.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Spatula: This is one of those kitchen tools that is not used as a verb, and the word is Latin for a flat piece.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Colander: It is a bowl with holes for draining, and it has no verb use.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Sawhorse: It's a noun and no one sawhorses a piece of wood.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Stapler: Stapling is the verb, but the tool itself has a noun form and not a verb.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Thimble: It protects a finger when sewing, and to thimble is not used as a verb.
Tools whose names are also verbs.Anvil: It's a noun only; the verb for using it is to forge or hammer.

Semiconductor companies.Intel: Founded in 1968 by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, it released the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, in 1971.
Semiconductor companies.AMD: Founded in 1969 as Intel's long-time x86 rival; its Ryzen chips helped revive its fortunes.
Semiconductor companies.Nvidia: It coined the term GPU with its GeForce 256 in 1999, and the AI boom has made it among the world's most valuable companies.
Semiconductor companies.Qualcomm: Maker of the Snapdragon phone chips, it was founded in 1985 and earns heavily from patent licensing.
Semiconductor companies.TSMC: Taiwan's TSMC makes chips for other companies and is the world's largest contract chipmaker; Morris Chang founded it in 1987.
Semiconductor companies.Texas Instruments: Jack Kilby invented the integrated circuit here in 1958, work that won him a Nobel Prize in 2000.
Semiconductor companies.Micron: An Idaho-based maker of memory chips, which are in many of the world's computers and phones.
Semiconductor companies.Broadcom: It makes Wi-Fi and networking chips and bought the software firm VMware for about $69 billion in 2023.
Semiconductor companies.Arm: Designs chips but does not make them; it licenses its designs, which power nearly every smartphone.
Semiconductor companies.MediaTek: A Taiwanese chip designer whose Dimensity processors power many of the world's smartphones.
Semiconductor companies.SK Hynix: A South Korean memory maker and a leading supplier of the high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips.
Semiconductor companies.Netflix: Started as a DVD-by-mail business in 1997, it streams video and doesn't sell chips.
Semiconductor companies.Oracle: Known for databases and cloud services, it owns Sun's old server line but sells software at heart.
Semiconductor companies.Adobe: Known for Photoshop and the PDF format, making software and not hardware.
Semiconductor companies.Salesforce: Cloud software maker founded in 1999 by Marc Benioff, famous for CRM tools.
Semiconductor companies.Spotify: Swedish music streaming service, which uses chips but doesn't make them.
Semiconductor companies.Uber: The ride-hailing company began in 2009 as UberCab.
Semiconductor companies.Zoom: Video-call service that boomed in 2020, a user of chips, not a maker.
Semiconductor companies.Dropbox: Began when Drew Houston forgot his USB drive on a bus trip, so he built a way to sync files online.
Semiconductor companies.Slack: Began as an internal tool for a failed game called Glitch; Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Semiconductor companies.Airbnb: Started in 2008 when its founders rented out air mattresses in their San Francisco apartment.
Semiconductor companies.Twitter: A social network now called X, bought by Elon Musk in 2022.
Semiconductor companies.PayPal: A payments company formed in 1998 by a merger, famous for its early founders' later ventures.
Semiconductor companies.Shopify: A Canadian commerce platform that began in 2004 as a snowboard shop's online store.

Legend of Zelda characters.Link: Players often call the hero Zelda by mistake. He is left-handed in most games, but the Wii Twilight Princess mirrored its world to make him right-handed.
Legend of Zelda characters.Zelda: The princess, not the hero, lends the series its name, honoring Zelda Fitzgerald. She often goes by a disguise, as in Sheik.
Legend of Zelda characters.Ganondorf: The series' recurring villain is the king of the Gerudo thieves, and he turns into the beastly Ganon, wielding the Triforce of Power.
Legend of Zelda characters.Epona: Link's horse, named after a Gaulish and Roman goddess of horses, and the first game she appeared in was Ocarina of Time in 1998.
Legend of Zelda characters.Navi: The fairy guiding Link in Ocarina of Time is famous for yelling 'Hey! Listen!', which became a meme for annoying hints.
Legend of Zelda characters.Impa: A Sheikah warrior who protects Princess Zelda, she appears across the series, from nursemaid to leader of her people.
Legend of Zelda characters.Midna: The imp from Twilight Princess seems mischievous but becomes Link's closest ally, and she is a fan favorite.
Legend of Zelda characters.Tingle: An adult man who believes he is a fairy, dressed in a green suit. Fans embraced him, and he got spin-off games, mostly released in Japan.
Legend of Zelda characters.Malon: The ranch girl from Ocarina of Time who teaches Link Epona's Song at Lon Lon Ranch, and her father is Talon.
Legend of Zelda characters.Darunia: The Goron chief in Ocarina of Time, who dances to Saria's Song and becomes sworn brothers with Link.
Legend of Zelda characters.Ruto: The Zora princess in Ocarina of Time, whom Link must carry inside Lord Jabu-Jabu's belly, and who calls him her fiance.
Legend of Zelda characters.Sheik: A trap: the mysterious Sheikah is actually Zelda in disguise in Ocarina of Time, and the reveal is one of the series' best twists.
Legend of Zelda characters.Skull Kid: Appearing in several games, he is the mischief-maker who wears Majora's Mask in Majora's Mask, and he also pops up in Ocarina's forest.
Legend of Zelda characters.Samus: A bounty hunter from Metroid, not Zelda, though she did cameo in Smash Bros. alongside Link.
Legend of Zelda characters.Kirby: The pink puffball is from HAL's own series, not Zelda, though he has fought Link in Smash.
Legend of Zelda characters.Ness: The EarthBound hero from Mother 2, a different Nintendo series, and he fights Link in Smash Bros. only.
Legend of Zelda characters.Marth: A Fire Emblem prince, and his Smash Bros. Melee debut helped bring the series west. He is from another game altogether.
Legend of Zelda characters.Pit: The angel archer from Kid Icarus, which came out in 1986, the same year as the first Zelda, but a different series.
Legend of Zelda characters.Fox: Star Fox's pilot, who flies an Arwing in his own space-shooter series, not in Hyrule's fields.
Legend of Zelda characters.Falco: The cocky bird pilot from Star Fox, who is always ready to argue with Fox, but isn't a Hyrule resident.
Legend of Zelda characters.Olimar: Captain Olimar is the tiny astronaut who leads Pikmin, in his own series, and his ship crashed on a mystery planet.
Legend of Zelda characters.Isabelle: The cheerful dog secretary from Animal Crossing joined Smash Bros. Ultimate in 2018, but she never lived in Hyrule.
Legend of Zelda characters.Wario: Mario's greedy rival, whose name mixes 'Mario' and the Japanese word 'warui' for bad. He's in his own series, not Zelda.
Legend of Zelda characters.Daisy: Princess of Sarasaland, introduced in Super Mario Land in 1989, a Mario character rather than a Zelda one.

Computer input devices.Keyboard: The QWERTY layout dates to the 1870s typewriters and was long believed to be designed to prevent jams, though the truth is more tangled.
Computer input devices.Mouse: Douglas Engelbart demonstrated the first one in 1968, a wooden shell with wheels, and called it a mouse because its cord looked like a tail.
Computer input devices.Microphone: Besides recording speech, it lets you control computers by voice. Emile Berliner patented an early carbon version in 1877.
Computer input devices.Webcam: The first webcam, in 1991, pointed at a coffee pot at Cambridge so researchers could check whether any coffee was left.
Computer input devices.Scanner: Early flatbeds borrowed the 1950s idea of turning images into digital values, and the very first scan was a picture of a baby in 1957.
Computer input devices.Joystick: Early aviators' control sticks gave it its name, and the stick moved from cockpits into 1970s arcades and home consoles like the Atari 2600.
Computer input devices.Touchpad: Laptop pads sense the electrical charge of your fingertip, which is why they ignore a plain plastic pen or most gloves.
Computer input devices.Stylus: The word comes from the Latin for a pointed writing tool that Romans used to scratch letters into wax tablets.
Computer input devices.Game controller: The directional pad was invented by Nintendo's Gunpei Yokoi for the 1980s Game & Watch, to replace the clumsy joystick.
Computer input devices.Trackball: Invented in 1946 for a British naval radar system, it's basically an upside-down mouse that predates the real mouse by decades.
Computer input devices.Barcode reader: The first scanned item was a pack of Wrigley's gum in 1974 at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, and the pack now sits in the Smithsonian.
Computer input devices.Graphics tablet: Artists draw on it with pressure-sensitive pens, and the earliest was the RAND Tablet from 1964.
Computer input devices.Monitor: A trap: it sends pictures out to you, so it is an output device, even though touchscreens muddy the line.
Computer input devices.Printer: It turns files into paper, so it's an output device. Early dot-matrix models famously screeched while they printed.
Computer input devices.Speakers: They send sound out, so they're output devices. The modern moving-coil loudspeaker design dates to the 1920s.
Computer input devices.Headphones: They deliver sound to you, so they're output only, unless a headset adds a mic. Early pairs weighed more than a pound.
Computer input devices.Projector: It throws the screen onto a wall, so it's an output device, a descendant of the 17th-century magic lantern.
Computer input devices.Plotter: A trap: it draws large technical diagrams with pens, so it's output only. Architects once relied on them for blueprints.
Computer input devices.Earbuds: They only play sound, so they count as output, unless built-in microphones are in the mix, which turn them into a headset.
Computer input devices.Subwoofer: It delivers the lowest bass frequencies, so it's output only, and shakes air at pitches you can feel more than hear.
Computer input devices.3D printer: It builds objects layer by layer, so it's an output device. Chuck Hull invented the process in the 1980s.
Computer input devices.Label printer: It prints stickers and shipping labels, so it is an output device. It prints with heat on special paper, so no ink is needed.
Computer input devices.Soundbar: It outputs sound, so it isn't an input device, and it squeezes several speakers into one slim bar so a TV can sound bigger.
Computer input devices.E-reader screen: It displays pages rather than collecting any data from you, so it's output. Its e-ink uses tiny charged capsules and sips power.

Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Brillig: The poem's first word. Humpty Dumpty explains it means four in the afternoon, when you begin broiling things for dinner.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Slithy: Humpty Dumpty says it blends "lithe" and "slimy", a perfect example of the portmanteau words Carroll made famous.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Toves: According to Humpty Dumpty, they look like badgers, lizards and corkscrews, nest under sundials and live on cheese.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Gyre: Unlike the rest, this is a real English word meaning to whirl in a circle. Humpty links it to the way a gyroscope spins.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Gimble: Humpty Dumpty says it means to make holes like a gimlet, which is what the toves do in the wabe.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Wabe: Humpty Dumpty defines it as the grass plot around a sundial, running a long way before it and a long way behind: way-be.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Mimsy: Humpty Dumpty explains it as "flimsy and miserable", which is how the borogoves feel in the poem.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Borogoves: A thin, shabby-looking bird with feathers sticking out all round, something like a live mop, according to Humpty Dumpty.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Frumious: Carroll's own preface says to blend "fuming" and "furious": if you think of both at once, you say frumious.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Bandersnatch: A fast, snapping creature that Carroll mentions here and in The Hunting of the Snark. It lent its name to a 2018 Black Mirror film.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Vorpal: Carroll never defined it, and it describes the sword that slays the Jabberwock. Fantasy games have since made it a staple for blades.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Galumphing: Carroll's blend of "gallop" and "triumphant" is the one invention here that stuck, and it's now in standard dictionaries.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Frabjous: Likely a mix of "fair", "fabulous" and "joyous", it comes from the king's victory cry, "O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!"
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Snozzcumber: Roald Dahl's knobbly, foul-tasting vegetable from The BFG. The giant eats it, and it is Dahl's invention, not Carroll's.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Whizzpopper: Dahl's word in The BFG for the giants' fizzy-drink-caused wind. A delightful coinage, but written about 100 years after Carroll.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Oobleck: Dr. Seuss's green goo that falls from the sky in Bartholomew and the Oobleck. It's now also a name for cornstarch-and-water slime.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Muggle: J. K. Rowling's word for a non-magical person, but in 1920s jazz slang, "muggles" meant marijuana. It is not from Carroll.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Quidditch: The broomstick sport Rowling invented for Harry Potter. It was never in Carroll's poem, though it sounds just as nonsensical.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Truffula: Dr. Seuss's tufted trees in The Lorax, chopped down by the Once-ler to make Thneeds. Seuss's nonsense, not Carroll's.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Sneetch: The star-bellied creatures of Dr. Seuss's 1953 story, a satire of prejudice. Another famous nonsense word, but not Carroll's.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Gobbledygook: Coined in 1944 by Texas congressman Maury Maverick to mock bureaucratic jargon, he said, like a turkey's gobble. Not Carroll.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Scrumdiddlyumptious: Roald Dahl's word for something delicious, from his books. A mouthful like Carroll's words, but it isn't from Jabberwocky.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Humbug: A real word for nonsense or deceit; Scrooge's "Bah, humbug!" made it famous. Carroll didn't use it here.
Words from the poem \"Jabberwocky\".Kerfuffle: A real English word for a fuss, from Scots "curfuffle". It sounds like nonsense but is not in Jabberwocky.

Star Wars planets.Tatooine: The Skywalkers' desert homeworld, named for Tataouine, a real Tunisian town where scenes were filmed.
Star Wars planets.Hoth: The ice world of The Empire Strikes Back was filmed near Finse, Norway, in 1979.
Star Wars planets.Endor: The forest moon of the Ewoks; Return of the Jedi's redwood scenes were shot in northern California.
Star Wars planets.Naboo: Padme's peaceful home; the royal palace scenes in The Phantom Menace used the Caserta palace in Italy.
Star Wars planets.Dagobah: The swamp world where Yoda hides, filmed on a studio set.
Star Wars planets.Coruscant: A city covering an entire planet and capital of the Republic; its name echoes 'coruscate', meaning to sparkle.
Star Wars planets.Alderaan: Leia's home, destroyed by the Death Star in A New Hope, killing billions in seconds.
Star Wars planets.Kashyyyk: The Wookiee homeworld, spelled with three y's and first seen in the 1978 Holiday Special.
Star Wars planets.Mustafar: A volcanic planet where Anakin and Obi-Wan duel in Revenge of the Sith.
Star Wars planets.Bespin: A gas giant with Cloud City, home of Lando Calrissian.
Star Wars planets.Jakku: The desert planet where Rey scavenged in The Force Awakens, partly filmed in Abu Dhabi.
Star Wars planets.Kamino: A stormy ocean world where the clone army was grown, in Attack of the Clones.
Star Wars planets.Vulcan: Spock's home in Star Trek, a different universe; the planet's name is also an old hypothetical planet once sought inside Mercury's orbit.
Star Wars planets.Arrakis: The desert planet of Dune, sole source of the spice melange; Frank Herbert's 1965 novel influenced Tatooine.
Star Wars planets.Pandora: The moon in Avatar, a satellite of the fictional gas giant Polyphemus, far from any Star Wars world.
Star Wars planets.Krypton: Superman's doomed home world; krypton is also a real element, a noble gas used in some lighting.
Star Wars planets.Gallifrey: Home of the Time Lords in Doctor Who, a planet with a burnt-orange sky, not a Star Wars world.
Star Wars planets.Romulus: The Star Trek home of the Romulans, named for Rome's legendary founder Romulus.
Star Wars planets.Cybertron: The metal homeworld of the Transformers, from a different franchise entirely, not Star Wars.
Star Wars planets.Mongo: Flash Gordon's planet in the 1934 comic strip, which inspired George Lucas to create Star Wars.
Star Wars planets.Skaro: Home planet of the Daleks in Doctor Who, a war-ravaged world far from the Star Wars galaxy.
Star Wars planets.Namek: The home of Piccolo in Dragon Ball Z, a green planet from Japanese manga, not Star Wars.
Star Wars planets.Magrathea: The Hitchhiker's Guide planet where custom planets are built, including Norway's fjords.
Star Wars planets.Tralfamadore: The alien planet in Kurt Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse-Five, whose inhabitants see all time at once.

Universal's classic movie monsters.Dracula: Bela Lugosi's 1931 performance set the look of the movie vampire, cape and accent included.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Frankenstein: In Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein is the doctor, not the monster, but Boris Karloff's 1931 film creature took the name.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Wolf Man: The 1941 film made the 'even a man who is pure in heart' rhyme famous, though it was written for the movie, not old folklore.
Universal's classic movie monsters.The Mummy: The 1932 film starring Boris Karloff was inspired partly by the craze that followed the 1922 discovery of King Tut's tomb.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Invisible Man: Claude Rains starred in 1933 and is famously unseen for much of the film, based on an H. G. Wells novel.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Gill-man: The Creature from the Black Lagoon (1954) was shot partly for 3D, and its design is still widely admired.
Universal's classic movie monsters.The Bride: Elsa Lanchester played her in 1935 with the white-streaked hair, though she appears on screen for only a few minutes.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Phantom of the Opera: Lon Chaney applied his own horrifying makeup for the 1925 film and kept it secret until the premiere.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Larry Talbot: Played by Lon Chaney Jr. in 1941, he is the tragic hero who reappears in later monster crossover films.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Imhotep: The Mummy's villain shares a name with a real architect and physician of about 2650 BCE, who designed the step pyramid.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Freddy Krueger: The 1984 slasher from A Nightmare on Elm Street belongs to the 1980s, not the 1930s Universal cycle.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Jason Voorhees: Jason did not wear his hockey mask until the third Friday the 13th film.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Michael Myers: The 1978 Halloween mask was reportedly a Captain Kirk mask, painted white.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Chucky: A doll possessed by a killer's soul, from Child's Play (1988), not a Universal monster.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Pennywise: Stephen King's shape-shifting clown from the 1986 novel It, not part of Universal's classic cycle.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Ghostface: The Scream killer's mask was a commercial costume found by chance while scouting a location.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Leatherface: The cannibal of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974), loosely inspired by killer Ed Gein.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Pinhead: Clive Barker's Hellraiser cenobite from the 1980s, a very modern horror.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Jigsaw: The Saw villain, from a 2004 film made on a tiny budget.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Candyman: Based on a Clive Barker story, the 1992 film moved the legend to Chicago.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Samara: The girl from The Ring, an American remake of Japan's Ringu.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Annabelle: The possessed doll of the Conjuring films; the real Annabelle was a Raggedy Ann, not the porcelain film version.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Norman Bates: Hitchcock's Psycho killer from 1960 is a human horror, not a creature feature.
Universal's classic movie monsters.Hannibal Lecter: The cannibal psychiatrist from Silence of the Lambs; Anthony Hopkins won an Oscar for about 16 minutes on screen.
